what_it_does: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) learn by passing information between connected nodes in a graph — think of friends-of-friends in a social network. A Dynamic GNN (DGNN) does this on a graph that changes over time, like a social graph where friendships appear and disappear. The typical approach re-runs the entire computation pipeline from scratch each time the graph changes, even if only a handful of edges shifted. This generates mountains of temporary data that must flow in and out of the slow off-chip memory chip (called DRAM), which is a major bottleneck. I-DGNN avoids this by mathematically reformulating the update — the difference between two consecutive graph snapshots — as a standalone chain of matrix multiplications that can be computed independently, so only what actually changed needs to move through the pipeline. A reconfigurable hardware accelerator is then designed to handle both this lightweight update path and the standard full-graph path, keeping data local and reducing expensive off-chip memory traffic.
